issues.description: The authors claim they 'utilized a prospective research design to understand which features in text communications predicted suicide attempt, overcoming the power issues of a true prospective study design.' However, this is fundamentally a retrospective design: participants retrospectively identified past episodes and the researchers then examined text messages from those periods. The text data itself may have been generated prospectively (i.e., in real time), but the identification of episodes and the analytic framework are entirely retrospective. Calling this a 'prospective research design' is misleading and overstates the strength of the causal inferences that can be drawn.
issues.quote: By reconstructing the timeline of recent suicidal behaviors through a retrospective clinical interview, we utilized a prospective research design to understand which features in text communications predicted suicide attempt, overcoming the power issues of a 'true' prospective study design.

issues.description: The study includes interrupted and aborted attempts, as well as incidents where 'no physical attempt was enacted but in which participants considered their planning or actions to constitute a higher level of suicidal intent than suicide ideation.' This means the 'attempt' category conflates qualitatively different events (actual ingestion/self-harm vs. driving to a bridge but not jumping). This heterogeneity in the key predictor variable undermines construct validity and may dilute or distort observed effects. The authors acknowledge this but do not analyze sensitivity to this classification decision.
issues.quote: Note that reported 'suicide attempts' also included incidents in which no physical attempt was enacted but in which participants considered their planning or actions to constitute a higher level of suicidal intent than 'suicide ideation' so they subjectively endorsed making an attempt on the screener questions.

issues.description: The entire within-subjects design depends on accurate retrospective identification and dating of episodes. While the authors note 90.3% of episodes were rated as 'very certain' or 'somewhat certain,' this is self-reported confidence, not validated accuracy. 'Somewhat certain' (may be off by a few days) is problematic for a 14-day window, as misalignment of even a few days could substantially alter the temporal slope analyses. No external validation of episode dates was conducted.
issues.quote: Participants were generally confident about the accuracy of the dates they selected, rating 90.3% of episodes as 'very certain' (i.e., exact days) or 'somewhat certain' (i.e., may be off by a few days).

issues.description: The study ran a large number of tests across multiple outcome variables (at least 12 omnibus tests plus numerous pairwise comparisons) without any correction for multiple comparisons. The authors justify this by citing Rothman (1990) and arguing the study is underpowered, but several of the significant results are at marginal p-values (e.g., anger interaction p=.049, positive emotion vs. ideation interaction p=.049, first-person pronoun vs. depressed p=.035). These would likely not survive even modest correction. The decision not to correct inflates Type I error risk substantially, and the justification that maximal random effects compensate is not statistically equivalent to a multiple comparisons correction.
issues.quote: we decided not to artificially suppress Type I error (i.e., using a multiple comparisons correction) but rather view any significant results in light of these caveats

issues.description: Table 1 reports iatrogenic change in 'Desire to die' as 0.20 (positive value, suggesting an increase from pre to post), but the text states 'desire to die from pre (M=0.82) to post (M=0.61) significantly decreased slightly, t(32)=2.23, p=.033.' The means show a decrease of 0.21, but the table shows +0.20. The sign in the table appears to be reversed (should be -0.21 or -0.20). Similarly, mood change is listed as -0.20 in the table but the means (6.33 to 6.12) show a decrease of 0.21, and the text says mood 'did not significantly change.' The inconsistency in sign and magnitude between the table and text is confusing.
issues.quote: desire to die from pre (M=0.82, SD=1.10) to post (M=0.61, SD=0.90) significantly decreased slightly, t(32)=2.23, p=.033

issues.subcategory: Discrepancy between results and discussion on anxiety
issues.description: In the Results section for Primary Analysis 1, the text states 'No significant effects by episode type emerged for more general emotional content (i.e., positive emotion, negative emotion, emotional tone) or other specific emotions/constructs (i.e., anxiety, anger, death).' However, in the Discussion, the authors state 'results indicated that the period of high risk just before a suicide attempt was associated with messages indicating greater anxiety and sadness.' The anxiety finding is not supported by the reported results (χ²(3)=3.62, p=.306 for means; χ²(3)=2.31, p=.511 for slopes). This is a direct contradiction between sections.
issues.quote: results indicated that the period of high risk just before a suicide attempt was associated with messages indicating greater anxiety and sadness

issues.subcategory: Severe sample attrition and selection bias in SMS data
issues.description: Of 33 participants, only 27 had any SMS data, and only 15 had SMS data from at least one suicide attempt episode. Of 293 total episodes collected, only 134 (46%) contained SMS data. This massive data loss is non-random (e.g., iPhone encryption, lack of cloud backups, new phones) and could introduce systematic bias. Participants who retained more text data may differ systematically from those who did not (e.g., in technology use patterns, age of phone, socioeconomic status). The effective sample for the key comparison (attempt episodes) is very small.
issues.quote: Among the episodes queried during the lab interview, 134 (46%) episodes contained SMS data, collected from 27 different participants. Among these 27 participants, 15 had data from at least one reported suicide attempt

issues.description: The authors state that the maximal random effects model for Analysis 2 did not converge, and they simplified the random effects structure by retaining only a by-participant slope for episode type. This is a significant departure from the planned maximal model and the Barr et al. (2013) recommendation they cite. The removal of random slopes for day and the episode-by-day interaction means the model may not adequately account for individual differences in temporal trajectories, potentially inflating Type I error for the interaction terms that are the primary focus of Analysis 2.
issues.quote: Models with the full set of random slopes did not converge; therefore, only a by-participant slope of episode type was included in the final model.

issues.description: The sample is predominantly female (84.8%), White (60.6%), college-aged (M=20.4 years), and college-educated (94% some college). This is a highly specific demographic that does not represent the population most at risk for suicide death (middle-aged and older White males). The authors do not adequately discuss how this limits generalizability. Additionally, the sample was recruited partly from a university participant pool, which may further limit representativeness.
issues.quote: Most of the participants were female, White, and college-aged.

issues.subcategory: LIWC limitations for text message analysis
issues.description: LIWC was designed for analysis of standard written text, not SMS messages which contain abbreviations, slang, emojis, non-standard spelling, and very short messages. The authors acknowledge that LIWC cannot handle negation ('not happy' counted as positive emotion) but do not discuss how SMS-specific language features might systematically bias LIWC scores. Short messages may produce unreliable LIWC percentage scores due to small word counts, and the conversion to proportions may not fully address this issue.
issues.quote: One weakness of this approach is that examining single words in isolation can fail to capture the semantic context of the word (e.g., 'not happy' would count as 'positive emotion' because negation is not accounted for)

issues.description: The study compares language during different episode types, but these episodes likely occurred at different calendar times and potentially different life stages. Confounds such as relationship status, academic stress, medication changes, life events, and even changes in texting habits over time are not controlled for. The within-subjects design helps with stable individual differences but does not address time-varying confounds. Any observed differences could reflect contextual factors correlated with but not caused by suicide risk.
issues.quote: Critically, classifications of these reported episodes became the basis of the study's within-subjects design, with episode type serving as our main predictor variable and language characteristics of text messages during the episodes as the outcome variables.

issues.subcategory: Power analysis based on inappropriate effect sizes
issues.description: The power analysis relies on large effect sizes from between-subjects studies (d=0.88-1.52) to justify the sample size for a within-subjects design. The authors acknowledge this mismatch but proceed with the assumption anyway. Within-subjects effect sizes for these constructs are unknown and could be substantially smaller. Furthermore, the effective sample for attempt episodes (n=15 with SMS data, containing only 21 attempts) is even smaller than the planned n=30, making the study severely underpowered even for large effects.
issues.quote: We determined that a sample size of 30 suicide attempters (representing 60 attempts but only 20 with collected, usable SMS data, divided by the design effect) would provide enough power to detect only large effect sizes

issues.description: Social engagement was operationalized solely as ratios and counts of sent vs. received messages. This is a very crude proxy for the theoretical constructs of thwarted belongingness and perceived burdensomeness from the interpersonal theory of suicide. Message volume does not capture the quality, content, or nature of social interactions. The authors acknowledge this limitation but it represents a fundamental mismatch between the theoretical construct and its operationalization.
issues.quote: we only examined aggregate information about incoming and outgoing messages and were not able to examine more fine-grained details about these interactions, such as who was initiating conversations, whether certain texts to participants were going unanswered

issues.subcategory: Missing details on number of attempts with SMS data
issues.description: The paper reports 21 attempts with corresponding SMS data from 15 participants (13 with single attempts, 14 with multiple). However, 13+14=27, not 15. These numbers appear to refer to different subsets (27 total participants with any SMS data vs. 15 with attempt SMS data), but the reporting is confusing. Additionally, the exact number of episodes per type that had SMS data is not clearly reported, making it difficult to evaluate the balance and power of comparisons.
issues.quote: Among attempters with SMS data, 13 participants reported a single lifetime attempt and 14 reported multiple (M=1.74, SD=0.86). Among the 21 attempts with corresponding SMS data

issues.description: The text states '13 participants reported a single lifetime attempt and 14 reported multiple' among 'attempters with SMS data.' This sums to 27 participants, but earlier the text states only 15 participants had data from at least one suicide attempt. If these 27 refer to all 33 participants (not just those with SMS data), this should be clarified. The mean of 1.74 attempts with SD=0.86 also seems inconsistent with 13 having exactly 1 attempt and 14 having multiple, as the mean would need to be higher if 14/27 had ≥2 attempts.
issues.quote: Among attempters with SMS data, 13 participants reported a single lifetime attempt and 14 reported multiple (M=1.74, SD=0.86).

issues.subcategory: Lack of blinding in episode classification
issues.description: The experimenter who conducted the interview to classify episodes was presumably aware of the study hypotheses. There is no mention of blinding in the episode classification process. Given that episode classification is the foundation of the entire analysis, experimenter bias in probing for or classifying episodes could systematically affect results. Additionally, participants knew the study was about suicide, which could influence their retrospective recall and classification of episodes.
issues.quote: participants were interviewed by the experimenter and asked to identify a number of episodes, including dates of past suicide attempts

issues.description: While the 14-day episode window was described as based on prior research, the authors also report using visual inspection of loess-smoothed plots to determine when changes were most pronounced, finding changes 'most notably and often around 7 days prior.' This data-driven approach to selecting the analysis window introduces researcher degrees of freedom. The choice of window length directly affects the slope estimates in Analysis 2, and no sensitivity analyses across different window lengths are reported in the main text.
issues.quote: temporal visualizations, using a smoother (loess) function, were constructed for each variable of interest and consisted of graphs plotting daily means for the given variable during the 30 days prior to and following the attempt. Although highly variable across variables, changes tended to occur most notably and often around 7 days prior to the suicide attempt.

issues.description: Despite the authors providing OSF materials, there is no mention of pre-registration of hypotheses, analysis plans, or outcome variables. Given the large number of outcome variables tested, the exploratory nature of many analyses, and the data-driven decisions made (e.g., time window selection, random effects simplification), pre-registration would have been important for distinguishing confirmatory from exploratory findings.
issues.quote: Numerous aspects of this research were exploratory by nature.

issues.description: The study uses retrospective data to identify associations between language features and episode types, yet the abstract and discussion repeatedly frame findings as evidence for 'real-time digital markers of suicide risk' and 'real-time digital biomarkers.' The study design cannot establish that these patterns would be detectable in real time, as the analysis depends on knowing when the attempt occurred. The term 'biomarker' is also inappropriate for linguistic features of text messages.
issues.quote: Results suggest private electronic communication has the potential to provide real-time digital markers of suicide risk.

issues.description: For sadness in Analysis 1, attempt episodes were significantly higher than ideation (z=2.64, p=.008) but NOT higher than depressed or positive mood episodes. This is a counterintuitive pattern: attempts differ from ideation but not from depressed or positive mood. The authors note this means sadness is 'not unique to suicide attempts,' but the pattern itself (higher than ideation but not different from depressed/positive) suggests possible issues with the comparison or the small sample sizes for certain episode types rather than a meaningful psychological pattern.
issues.quote: attempt episodes were significantly higher in sad words compared to ideation (z=2.64, p=.008), but not compared to depressed or positive mood (zs=1.07-1.09, ps=.277-.285)

issues.description: Attempt episodes are defined as the 14 days BEFORE the attempt, creating a natural temporal directionality toward a specific event. Other episode types (ideation, depressed, positive) are simply 14-day periods without a comparable terminal event. This structural asymmetry means that any natural temporal variation in language could appear as a 'slope' difference for attempt episodes simply because they are anchored to a specific event, while other episodes have no such anchor. This is a fundamental design confound for the slope analyses.
issues.quote: using the two-week period prior to the attempt as a 'suicide attempt episode'... 2) two-week episodes of suicide ideation (not resulting in a suicide attempt); 3) two-week episodes of depressed mood or high stress (not resulting in suicide ideation or attempt); and 4) two-week episode of positive mood

issues.description: Only 46% of reported episodes had SMS data, and the missingness is likely non-random across episode types. Older episodes (which may be more likely to be attempt episodes given recruitment criteria requiring past attempts) would be less likely to have SMS data due to phone changes. The 12 participants who contributed non-attempt episodes but no attempt episodes create an unbalanced design. The impact of this differential missingness on the mixed-effects estimates is not discussed.
issues.quote: Among these 27 participants, 15 had data from at least one reported suicide attempt; the other 12 participants contributed data from non-suicide attempt episodes and were still included in the analyses.

issues.subcategory: Missing ICC and variance component information
issues.description: For mixed-effects models with multiple random effects (participant, episode, message), the intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) and variance components are not reported. These are essential for understanding how much variance exists at each level and for evaluating whether the random effects structure is appropriate. Without this information, it is impossible to assess the effective sample size or the degree of clustering.
issues.quote: A mixed-effects method was selected because of its well-established advantages in terms of producing more accurate effect estimates

issues.subcategory: Episode classification based on subjective self-report
issues.description: The classification of episodes into attempt, ideation, depressed, and positive categories relies entirely on participants' retrospective self-report during a single interview. There is no corroboration from medical records, clinical charts, or collateral informants. Given that the distinction between 'attempt' and 'ideation' is the critical comparison, and participants' subjective interpretation determines classification, misclassification could substantially affect results. The authors note that some 'attempts' involved no physical action, further blurring the boundary.
issues.quote: classification of episode type depended on participants' interpretations of whether their behaviors qualified as a specific type of event

issues.subcategory: Death words omnibus significant but no pairwise comparisons significant
issues.description: For death words in Analysis 2, the omnibus test was significant (χ²(3)=9.47, p=.024), but none of the pairwise comparisons between attempt and other episode types reached significance (ps=.067-.739). This pattern suggests the omnibus effect may be driven by differences between non-attempt episode types rather than by attempt episodes being distinct, yet the authors frame this in the context of attempt episodes. This also raises questions about the appropriateness of the omnibus test or potential issues with the pairwise comparison corrections.
issues.quote: There was also a significant interaction for death words, χ2(3)=9.47, p=.024. However, there were no significant differences in change over time for attempt compared to all other episodes (zs=0.33-1.83, ps=.067-.739)

issues.description: 71% of the reported attempt incidents did not result in any physical harm, and only 29% involved some action with physical consequences. This suggests many of the 'attempts' were of relatively low lethality, limiting generalizability to more medically serious suicide attempts or completed suicides. The communication patterns preceding low-lethality attempts may differ substantially from those preceding high-lethality attempts.
issues.quote: 29% of incidents involved some action being taken in which some physical harm was caused... while 71% of incidents did not result in any physical harm (e.g., driving to high place, such as a bridge, but deciding not to jump)

issues.description: Digital phenotyping typically refers to real-time, passive collection of digital data to characterize behavior. This study retrospectively analyzed historical text messages, which is fundamentally different from real-time digital phenotyping. The framing of this work as digital phenotyping overstates the methodological approach and conflates retrospective text analysis with prospective passive monitoring.
issues.quote: The ubiquity of mobile technology, including private text data, offers ripe opportunities for the real-time quantification of individual-level human behavior, known as 'digital phenotyping'

issues.description: With 189,478 messages across 134 episodes, the average is approximately 1,400 messages per episode. However, the distribution of messages across episodes and participants is not reported. If some episodes have very few messages while others have thousands, this could create influential observations in the mixed-effects models. Information about message length (word count) distributions is also not provided, which is relevant given that LIWC scores from very short messages may be unreliable.
issues.quote: Across all episodes, 189,478 text messages were collected and analyzed, ranging between on average about 1,200-1,600 text messages per episode.

issues.subcategory: Inclusion of participants without attempt SMS data
issues.description: 12 of 27 participants with SMS data did not have data from any suicide attempt episode. Including these participants in the mixed-effects models means they contribute to estimates of random effects and non-attempt episode parameters but not to the critical attempt comparisons. While mixed models can handle this, it means the key comparison (attempt vs. other) is based on only 15 participants, further reducing effective power for the primary research question.
issues.quote: the other 12 participants contributed data from non-suicide attempt episodes and were still included in the analyses

issues.description: The authors mention 'Additional analyses were performed to examine the same set of outcome variables but in different ways to examine the robustness of the primary results' in Supplement 3, but do not summarize whether these supplementary analyses supported or contradicted the primary findings. This makes it impossible to evaluate the robustness of the reported results without accessing supplementary materials.
issues.quote: Additional analyses were performed to examine the same set of outcome variables but in different ways to examine the robustness of the primary results and to see if the pattern of results changed. Those analyses are available in Supplement 3 online.
